html:
A life-size bronze statue of a chariot driver found at Delphi, made around 478 to 474 BCE. It was part of a group with a chariot and horses, set up to celebrate a win in the chariot race at the Pythian Games.

An inscription names the donor as Polyzalus, a ruler of Gela in Sicily and brother of Gelon of Syracuse. The young driver stands calmly in a long robe, holding the reins. His eyes, inlaid with glass and stone, and his copper lips and lashes still survive.

Most Greek bronzes were melted down for metal, so very few survive. This one did because an earthquake and rockfall buried it, probably in 373 BCE. French excavators found it in 1896.

It is a prime example of the Severe Style, the plain, serious stage between archaic and Classical sculpture, seen also at the Temple of Zeus at Olympia. It now stands in the Delphi museum, near the sanctuary of the Oracle.
